title: The whole tractate
hookLine: sixty-four pages read; the siyum closes with a special Kaddish
tomorrow: you finished a tractate. so what's on the table?

cards: Graduation is called commencement, a word for beginning, said on the day something ends. Berakhot runs from page two to page sixty-four.

Page two, because the Talmud's pages start there; some say it's a reminder that nobody ever truly starts at the beginning. And when the last page is done, the siyum closes with a Kaddish you don't hear on an ordinary day.
So: finished, or begun? Inside the tradition, both answers have a voice.

teach.b: First voice: it's finished, and that matters. A siyum, a completion, is a real occasion. People stop, read the last lines aloud, say the hadran, and celebrate.
A whole tractate, learned from its first question to its last word, is something you can hold. It deserves a moment that says: you did this. Second voice: it's never finished.
Rabbi Tarfon says in Pirkei Avot: it isn't on you to complete the work, and you aren't free to quit it.

teach.h: THE FIRST LINES OF THE NEXT.
teach.b: There's a custom, at a siyum, of reading the first lines of the next tractate before the celebration ends, so the learning never actually closes. Now listen to the Kaddish they say.

teach.h: A KADDISH OF A WORLD MADE NEW.
teach.b: This special Kaddish of the siyum speaks of a world that will be made new, and of God giving life to the dead. Something to tell a friend tonight: a form of that same Kaddish is also said at a burial.
The words for the end of a book are the words for the end of a life, and both talk about renewal. So both voices win. The finish is real, and it's celebrated.
The finish is also a door, and the custom walks right through it. A whole tractate isn't a trophy on a shelf. It's a ground to stand on for the next one.

how: At a siyum the learners read the tractate's last lines, say the hadran, and recite a special Kaddish; some also read the opening lines of the next tractate before the meal.

practice: When a Kaddish is said, the people listening answer it. Say the answer once, slowly, out loud: amen, yehei shmei rabba mevarakh, may His great name be blessed forever.
Then sit for a moment with the word amen, the yes that answers a prayer.

wordCard.voice: The whole tractate. Berakhot, read from its first page to its last, and the custom of beginning again at once.

orig.note: Aramaic: may His great name be blessed. the answer to every Kaddish.

carryVoice: The line to keep: finished and begun, at the same time, in the same breath. Forty-nine of fifty.

sources.ref: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:16 (Rabbi Tarfon: it is not upon you to complete the work, nor are you free to desist from it)
